**Verdict:** Yes. Admit the weaknesses your prospect is already thinking, and say them before they do. Admit the flaw first, put "but" after it, and put the claim you want believed after the "but". He would give up some promise to get more trust.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). He addresses this directly for ads, and again for sales calls.

**How to word it**
1. **List the flaws.** He says to "write down all of the flaws all the things that people complain about the things that you know you could do better and claim them" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 15:03; [watch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s)). The reason is that "the prospect is already thinking them", so claiming them first earns you trust.
2. **Put the flaw before the "but".** In his words, "the statement that comes after the word but is the part that is the thing you want them to believe" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 13:44). The order matters. If you say "these markers write four times longer than others but they smell like crap", you stress the smell. Say the smell first and the longer writing second.
3. **Keep the admission true and believable.** It has to be "true and believable and damaging to you". A fake flaw like "we care too much" won't work.
4. **Use his example wording:**
   - "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 15:03)
   - "our systems are incredibly boring but they work" (same passage)
   - For a gym: "our gym has honestly pretty terrible parking our AC is kind of on and off i don't have the best equipment but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 15:39)
5. **Make it funny if you can.** "If you can do with humor you get even more bonus points" (same passage).
6. **Use the same move on calls and landing pages when the offer sounds too good to be true.** He says: "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad" ([[yt-MH-IMJxbUY4]] @ 19:42; [watch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1182s)). Then list what's bad about it. He says this lets prospects "self-qualify". The people who still want it have heard the downsides and don't mind them. He does this because those prospects want the benefit and just don't believe it.

**Why he'd say it**
- Trust is worth more than the promise: "what you'll sacrifice in promise you'll gain in trust and trust trumps promise" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 13:09; [watch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s)). He adds "I would rather always sacrifice promise to gain trust" (same passage).
- He rates it as his strongest tactic: "nothing more powerful than damaging admissions" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 12:30). He also says "of course your product isn't perfect say so".
- It makes you stand out. "If you want to stand out in a crowded marketplace tell the truth" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 15:39).
- It matches his other rules. He says to call out who the ad isn't for, which "polarize[s] the customers who are the right customer to move even more towards you" ([[yt-JDR-R--4HhM]] @ 6:15; [[marketing/copywriting/calling-out-your-audience]]). A flaw admission does the same job by filtering.

**What he's done:** He says his own sites are ugly, which is the "ugly as hell but they convert" line. He uses the Eminem rap-battle story as an illustration. The research he cites on admitting bias is unnamed, so treat it as an illustration, not his data. The vault doesn't show an actual ad of his that uses this.

**What would change his answer:** He would drop an admission that hits the thing the customer is buying. The flaw has to be about something they care less about than the claim after "but", like parking against fun sessions. Saying "our product doesn't work" is not what he means. Putting the admission after the claim would also reverse the effect. This part is my reading of his "but" mechanic, not something he said outright.

**Where I'd add a note of my own:** His advice assumes you have a real strength to put after the "but". If you can't finish "…but ___" with something strong and provable, the admission just advertises the weakness. He pairs it with proof elsewhere ([[marketing/copywriting/proof-and-authority]]).

**Verdict:** Aim for under 10% monthly churn, which he calls best-in-class. About 20% is typical. Worry when more than 3 in 10 members leave each month. At that point he says retention is the first thing to fix, ahead of ads and new features. He also says to watch churn by tenure rather than as one average, because new members always churn the most.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). He gives these numbers himself, but they all come from one talk, and the benchmarks are Skool platform averages.

**Why he'd say it**
- Typical is about 80% monthly retention and best is under 10% churn. This is from the leaf's summary of the talk, not a verbatim line ([[business/retention/measuring-churn]]).
- The worry line is 70% retention: "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 1:39; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s)
- Small improvements pay off a lot: "you didn't just get a 10 or 12% boost, you got a double in the LTV per customer" (@ 2:13). Halving churn doubles lifetime value.
- Churn depends on tenure, so the average misleads: "the biggest rule is that churn drops dramatically with time" (@ 3:19).
  - The first big drop is at day 90: "if you keep someone 90 days… it drops to around 10% or less" (@ 3:53).
  - The second is at month six: "it goes from like 10% to 2%" (@ 3:53).
- He says to stop trying to push the average down: "How do I get someone to stay past day 90? How do I get these people to stay past month six?" (@ 4:24). He admits he used to obsess over the average himself.
- He wants a plan for month one: "have a very specific strategy for getting people past the first month cuz that's the biggest month of churn" (@ 4:57). He also says "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks" (@ 4:24).
- Track joins against cancels every month, and label the business growing, flat or declining (@ 0:33). Churn only matters relative to new members.

**What he'd tell you to do about it** (all from the same talk)
- **By day 90:** deliver an outcome or a behavior change. By month six, the member should have connected with other people in the community (@ 5:31).
- **Overwhelm:** "The number one reason people churn, outside of price, is overwhelm" (@ 9:18). Doing less retains more.
- **Presence:** owners who show up daily had "significantly higher retention" (@ 13:39).
- **Annual plans:** "annual always has lower churn than monthly" (@ 15:52).
- **Cancellations:** message everyone who cancels and tag their reason. Every 20 or so cancels, fix the top one or two reasons ([[business/retention/cancellation-feedback]]).

**What would change his answer**
- **Community age:** if your community is under 90 days old, your churn will look inflated. No one has reached the low-churn months yet. Read churn by cohort (members who joined in the same month) rather than panicking at the blended number. He says this himself, per the leaf's caveats.
- **Business type:** the benchmarks fit online and consumer services, not things like insurance premiums or alarm systems.
- **Source bias:** the data comes from Skool, which he co-founded and promotes ([[profile]]). Treat the exact thresholds as rough rules of thumb. The vault has no second source that confirms them.

**Verdict:** Pay it off. Hormozi would have you clear the $60k aggressively, ideally from cash flow over the next four to five months. He'd keep growing at the same time, and he'd fund growth from profit rather than from debt. His reason is that debt adds risk, and "risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due."

**Based on:** said it. He gave almost this exact answer to a consulting client with $60k of debt. The one part that goes beyond that is the "keep cash for growth" side, which I've marked below (confidence: medium).

**Why he'd say it**
- He asked the owner of ProShine (an air-duct cleaning business) how fast they planned to clear their $60k. The owner said four to five months. Hormozi said: "Okay, good. That's one of those things that like I'd say this is more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:37, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s)
- He places himself on the Ramsey end of the spectrum: "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side." (@ 8:37)
- His one argument is that debt adds risk: "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." He adds that "businesses have seasons, they have volatility" and that enduring companies like Chick-fil-A "operate debt free." (@ 9:10, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=550s)
- He asked why the debt was taken on: "A lot of times it's like cuz I wanted to grow faster." So he sees borrowing to grow as the usual trap. (@ 9:10)
- When he summarised the plan, "continue to pay off the debt" was priority #2, right behind a 10% price increase. (@ 30:45)
- It matches his wider rule of getting safe before taking swings: "get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible. Like do whatever you got to do to get your oxygen mask on." ([[yt-XGm2ERU9qtA]] @ 17:53)

**How the "keep cash for growth" side fits** (follows from what he said, confidence: medium)
1. His growth advice for that same client was price, funnel and ad creative first, and more ad spend only after those are fixed. A 10% price rise was worth about "a hundred plus thousand a year" for that business (@ 8:37). That money costs little and pays back faster than debt interest does, so you rarely need your debt-payoff cash to get it.
2. He does say to spend as much as you can on ads when the return is proven: "if you know that's where the money's coming from, by all means, spend more." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 11:21) He also says "you cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money." ([[yt-jfW6gL6hKhk]] @ 13:04)
3. In the ProShine plan he did both: he kept the debt payoff running and also told them to raise ad spend once the funnel was fixed. I'd expect the same for you. Pay down debt with a fixed share of monthly profit, and put into growth only the channels where you can show the return.

**What they've done:** he told a client with the same $60k to keep paying it down, and he put that on the priority list. He also says he went through the emotional barrier of spending $1,000 a day on ads himself, so he isn't against spending.

**What would change their answer**
- If you have a channel with trusted attribution and a high return (he mentions 10–30:1 for small businesses), he'd lean toward spending on it. Even then he'd probably pay the debt down at the same time rather than choose one.
- If you can't measure the return, he calls that "a data problem." That isn't a reason to spend the debt money.
- The vault doesn't say what interest rate the debt carries, or how much cash you'd have left after paying it. His case is about risk and not about rate math, so it may not carry over if your debt is cheap and your cash reserve is thin.
- His own stance is "more of an emotional thing," and it sits uneasily with his pro-risk talks. In June 2026 he described heavy debt as how fund managers get rich ([[tensions]]). He never reconciles the two, and the debt view comes from that one consult, so treat it as his rule of thumb for small operating businesses.

My one separate comment: a Ramsey-style rule fits less well if the debt is low-interest and paying it off would leave you without a cash buffer. Keeping a few months of expenses on hand is his "oxygen mask" logic too, and I'd do that before sending every spare dollar to the lender.

**Verdict:** Don't hold prices to protect an 82% close rate. Hormozi would say the 82% is the sign you're underpriced. He'd have you raise about 10% and keep going as long as you still close above roughly 65%.

**Based on:** said it. He addressed an HVAC-cleaning owner at this close rate and made this exact call. The math for your numbers is my own arithmetic.

**Why he'd say it**
- He reads a high close rate as a pricing signal: "So whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s)
- He rejects the premise that a higher price hurts closing. For a normal, non-luxury service, "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:00, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s)
- Underpricing can cost you sales: "they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale because it's so low price that they're like, 'Gosh, this guy seems like a run you know uh super seedy duct tape operation.'" ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:33, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s)
- At your size, price is a big lever: "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business is simply charging more because people actually believe you can deliver the service now." He puts that at businesses under roughly $3–5M. ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06)
- The decision rule is a break-even close rate, not fear: "We would have to believe that we're not going to drop to 65%. As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 8:06)

**What he's done:** In that consult (*Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes*), the owner was an HVAC-cleaning operator. His team had told him he was mispriced. The owner raised prices 23% and "that resulted in a higher close rate and more money." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 6:26, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=386s) Hormozi then proposed another 10%, to about $1,650 per unit, which he penciled at "roughly a 25% increase in net profit." He called it "more asking than telling."

**Your numbers (my arithmetic, not his):**
- At $1.2M and 38% net, you keep about $456k. A 10% raise at the same volume adds about $120k, which is a 26% profit increase. That matches his ~25% figure.
- Per-job profit rises from 0.38 to 0.48 of today's price, a factor of about 1.26. Break-even is therefore 82% ÷ 1.26, or about 65%. That is the same threshold he gave, so his math carries over to your business.
- You can lose about 17 points of close rate before the raise costs you money. Fewer closes also means fewer jobs to staff and supply, so the real cushion is a bit larger if your costs are mostly per-job.

**What would change his answer:** He'd want to know whether you already raised prices recently. His 10% came after the owner's 23% raise. If you've held flat for years, the vault suggests he'd push harder than 10%. The 65% figure was computed on that owner's economics, so confirm yours (it's about 65% on the numbers above). He'd also drop the idea if your 82% comes from a very narrow, pre-qualified lead flow that a higher price would break. The vault says nothing on that case, so that last point is my guess.

I'd add one line of my own, separate from his view. Raise in a measurable way, such as a 10% increase for 30 days while you track the close rate. His own "asking, not telling" framing points the same way.

**Hormozi doesn't tell this story. The host of the podcast does.**

The story is in the vault, in his April 2023 *Diary of a CEO* interview ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo). The interviewer tells it, and Hormozi only reacts to it. The vault holds auto-captions with no speaker labels, so I'm attributing the story from its content. It's about "my company" going public, and it ends with "we started our company which is now called flight story". That points to the host, Steven Bartlett. The profile page lists the episode as an interview with Bartlett. This isn't a Hormozi story, and the wiki has nothing on it.

**The story, as the host tells it**
- His company listed on a European exchange. Investment banks on the roadshow told him the exact same business would be worth four times more on the NASDAQ, so his net worth would be four times higher "just by taking the exact same business and moving it to a different Stock Exchange." ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:34:12)
- Later he looked for the industry where his skill set was scarcest and paid most. He settled on social media marketing and storytelling for companies about to IPO: "if you have a good story it can swing your valuation by hundreds of millions." The first company he worked with listed at about $3 billion. ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:34:43 to 1:35:17)
- The equity deal: he could help a local gym for "a th000 bucks" or take "7 million… as part of an equity deal" from a company heading into an IPO. He says the equity was "in the region of 7 to8 million" on IPO day for "nine months work." ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:35:17 to 1:35:51) The caption text is garbled in places, and the share price moved, so treat the numbers as approximate.
- He then founded Flight Story to apply the same skills to IPO and biotech clients. ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:36:23)

**What Hormozi says in response**
- He agrees with the lesson: "I thoroughly agree with everything you just said I also think that that's a skill I wish some just said it to me." ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:36:23)
- Later he ties it back to his leverage framework. The capital types run from friends and family to institutional money to public money, and "there's just significantly more capital in that." He mentions "the fact that the NASDAQ was Forex," the host's four-times point. ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]] @ 1:45:47) That fits his capital-as-leverage idea in [[business/leverage/types-of-leverage]].

Hormozi has not taken an IPO equity deal. The $7–8 million deal is the host's. I found no other mention of NASDAQ or IPOs by him in the vault's wiki or raw sources.

If you want his own take on this kind of deal, I can answer from his deal-structure pages, such as [[business/deal-structure/six-levels-of-getting-paid]] and [[business/deal-structure/risk-and-compensation]]. That would be an inference from his rules, not something he said about this story.

**Verdict:** The premise is wrong. Hormozi told the owner to do the opposite: go all in on door-to-door. Nothing in the vault shows him recommending Google Ads for this roofing company.

**Based on:** said it. The source is the roofing consult on Scale or Fail ("How I Would Build a $10M Service Business (If I Had to Start Over)", https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU). The owner's company was two months old, and he closed about one sale per 20 doors.

**What the vault shows**
- **Focus on the best channel:** "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 3:16, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=196s)
- **Door-knocking as an asset:** "that reliability of being able to just basically go get money um is something that a lot of entrepreneurs don't know how to do." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 3:16)
- **His recommendation:** "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 9:49, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s)
- **Don't get fancy:** "It's what you're good at." and "Like I don't think we need to be cute about this." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 10:21)
- **Scaling it:** "I think you building out this DDD army is like the clear straight shot." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 10:54). "DDD" is the auto-caption for "D2D".
- **Rep pay tied to effort:** "So, it's like how much money do you want to make? Just knock that many doors." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 10:54)
- **Follow-up:** "the first thing we said was go all in on door to door as primary growth engine." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 24:27)

The only "Google" in that transcript is a Google-review ask at 12:02, a customer follow-up tactic. It is not an ad channel. A raw-text search of the whole vault for "Google ads" turned up only general ad-creative material, nothing about roofing or door-knocking.

**Where the idea may have come from**
- **Another video:** You may be thinking of a different episode or guest. Tell me which one and I'll search for it.
- **Mixed-up advice:** The consult's other headline fix was raising the average ticket (3:07 in the chapter list). That may have blurred with ad advice.
- **Hormozi's general ad views:** The vault's advertising pages cover creative testing and landing pages, not a "stop door-knocking, buy Google Ads" rule.

**What would change his answer:** His reasoning was that door-knocking was this owner's proven, reliable channel and the highest return available to him right now. If the owner had no reliable closing channel, or door-knocking stopped paying, he'd presumably look at other channels. That is my inference, not something he said in this video.
